  • 1 tsp salt

Day 1 to ~Day 10Keeps forever

Change a Car Tire

Time 15–30 minTools: jack, lug wrench, spare
  • Spare tire (check pressure)

  5. Remove lug nuts and set aside. Pull the tire straight off.

  7. Lower the car, then tighten nuts firmly in a star pattern.
  8. Stow the flat and tools. Check spare pressure soon—most spares are temporary.

Never go under a car supported only by a jack.

Jump Start a Car

Time 10 minTools: jumper cables, another car
  • Jumper cables
  • Working car
  • Safety glasses (optional)
  1. Park the working car close, but not touching. Turn both cars off.
  2. Connect red clamp to positive (+) terminal of dead battery.
  3. Connect other red clamp to positive (+) of good battery.
  4. Connect black clamp to negative (-) of good battery.
  5. Connect other black clamp to a bare metal bolt on the dead car's engine block—not the battery.
  6. Start the working car, let it run a minute, then start the dead car.
  7. Once started, remove cables in reverse order: black from dead car, black from good, red from good, red from dead.
  8. Keep the revived car running for at least 20 minutes.

Never let clamps touch each other. Don't lean over the battery.

Keep Bananas From Ripening Too Fast

Active 2 min Makes 5–7 days

Ripe bananas give off ethylene gas, and they're sensitive to it too. So the trick is separating them and slowing that gas down.

  • 1 bunch bananas, still green-tipped
  • 1 roll plastic wrap or a beeswax wrap
  • 1 banana hanger (optional)
  • 1 cool, dark spot away from other fruit
  1. Wrap the crown (the top where they all join) tightly with plastic wrap. That's where most of the ethylene escapes.
  2. Separate the bananas from each other. They ripen faster when touching.
  3. Keep them at room temperature, out of direct sun. Fridge is fine once they're ripe, but the skin will go brown — the fruit inside stays good.
  4. Don't store near apples, avocados, or tomatoes. They're ethylene factories.

Already too ripe? Peel, slice, and freeze for smoothies. No waste, user_name.

Get Rid of Fruit Flies (For Good)

Active 5 min Makes 2–3 days

Fruit flies lay eggs in overripe produce and damp drains. Break the cycle and they vanish.

  • Apple cider vinegar, about 1/4 cup
  • 2 drops liquid dish soap

  4. Flush drains with boiling water or a vinegar-baking soda mix to kill eggs lurking in the gunk.
  5. Repeat daily until you see none for two days.

Prevention: rinse produce when you bring it home, and keep fruit in the fridge. user_name, you'll be fly-free by the weekend.

  3. Cross your right hand over your left, grabbing the bottom hem (point C) while still holding A and B.
  4. Lift and pull. The shirt will fold itself. Lay it down, tuck the sleeves, and you're done.

Season a Stainless Steel Pan

Prep 5 minTotal 15 minServes your future dinners

Stainless isn't nonstick, but you can make it behave. The trick is heat and fat, not a coating.

  • 1 stainless steel skillet, clean and dry
  • 1 tbsp high-smoke-point oil (grapeseed, canola, or avocado)
  • 1 paper towel
  • 1 thin slice of ginger (optional test)
  1. Set the pan over medium heat for 2 minutes. Sprinkle a few drops of water: if they bead and skate, it's ready.
  2. Add the oil and swirl to coat the bottom.
  3. Tilt the pan and wipe the oil around with the paper towel, leaving a thin film. It will smoke a little.
  4. Keep heating 2–3 more minutes until the oil darkens slightly and just begins to smoke.
  5. Turn off the heat. Let the pan cool, then wipe out the excess oil. It's now seasoned enough for eggs.
  6. Test with the ginger slice: if it slides, you're golden.
Why this works

The heat opens the microscopic pores in the steel, and the oil fills them, creating a temporary slick surface. Re-season every few uses.

Don't use olive oil for this—it burns before the pan is ready. Save it for finishing.

Fix a Running Toilet

  • 1 adjustable wrench
  • 1 sponge or towel
  • 1 bucket (just in case)
  1. Turn off the water supply valve behind the toilet. Flush to empty the tank.
  2. Sponge out remaining water. Unhook the old flapper from the overflow tube and chain.
  3. Take the old flapper to the hardware store and match it exactly.
  4. Install the new flapper: hook it onto the overflow tube, connect the chain with about ½ inch of slack.
  5. Turn the water back on. Let the tank fill and watch. If it still runs, adjust the chain or the float height.
  6. If water still runs, check the fill valve—sometimes a $10 part fixes it.
When to call a plumber

If the tank itself is cracked or the flange is broken, that's a bigger job. But 90% of running toilets are just the flapper.

Don't overtighten the flapper chain—it can lift the flapper and cause a slow leak.

  5. Preheat oven to 450°F (230°C) with the Dutch oven inside for 30 minutes.
  6. Carefully transfer dough (with parchment) into the hot pot. Cover and bake 30 minutes. Remove lid, bake 15 more minutes until deep golden.
  7. Cool on a rack before slicing. Try to wait.

Time does the work. The long rise develops gluten without muscle.

Deep Clean a Dishwasher

Time 30 minFrequency Monthly

If your glasses smell like wet dog, it's not the soap. It's the filter and the door gasket.

  • White vinegar, 1 cup
  • Baking soda, 1/2 cup
  • Old toothbrush
  • Dish soap and warm water
  • Microfiber cloth
  1. Empty it. Remove all dishes and silverware.
  2. Pull the filter. Twist and lift the bottom filter. Rinse under hot water, scrub with dish soap and toothbrush. This is where the gunk lives.
  3. Wipe the gasket. The rubber seal around the door collects food bits. Wipe with warm soapy water, then dry.
  4. Vinegar cycle. Put a cup of vinegar in a bowl on the top rack. Run a hot water cycle. No detergent.
  5. Baking soda sprinkle. Sprinkle baking soda on the bottom, run a short hot rinse. It deodorizes and gently scours.
  6. Dry and done. Leave the door cracked to air out.
Don't skip the filter. A clogged filter is the #1 cause of bad dishwasher smells. Clean it monthly.

Classic Vinaigrette

Prep 5 minMakes 3/4 cup

Three parts oil, one part acid. Shake it in a jar. That's the whole trick.

  • 3/4 cup olive oil
  • 1/4 cup red wine vinegar (or lemon juice)
  • 1 tsp Dijon mustard
  • 1 small garlic clove, minced
  • Salt and pepper
  1. Combine. Put vinegar, mustard, garlic, salt, and pepper in a jar with a tight lid.
  2. Shake. Shake hard for 10 seconds until it looks cloudy.
  3. Add oil. Pour in the olive oil. Shake again for 20–30 seconds. It'll emulsify into a creamy dressing.
  4. Taste. Dip a lettuce leaf. Adjust: more oil if too sharp, more vinegar if too flat, salt to wake it up.
  5. Store. Keep in the fridge up to a week. Shake before each use; separation is normal.

Build a Fire in a Fireplace (No Smoke in the Room)

  7. Spot-prime. Skip this and the patch will flash through the paint as a dull spot.

Sharpen a Kitchen Knife on a Whetstone

Time 15 minAngle 15–20°

A dull knife is the dangerous one, user_name. It slips. Ten minutes on a stone fixes that for months.

  • Combination whetstone, 1000/6000 grit
  • Water (most stones are soak-and-go)
  • A towel or non-slip mat
  • Your knife
  • Optional: a leather strop or honing rod
  1. Soak the 1000-grit side in water for 10–15 minutes until bubbles stop. Keep it wet the whole time.
  2. Set the stone on the towel, coarse side up, and hold it steady.
  3. Find the angle: lay the blade flat, then lift the spine about the thickness of two stacked coins. That's roughly 18°.
  4. Push the edge across the stone like you're slicing a thin layer off the top, heel to tip. Light pressure.
  5. Do 10 passes on one side, then 10 on the other. Alternate. Keep the angle locked — wobbling rounds the edge.
  6. Feel for a burr along the far side of the edge. A faint catch under your thumb means you're done on the coarse side.
  7. Flip the stone to 6000 grit. Same motion, but barely any pressure — this is polishing, not grinding.
  8. Rinse and dry the blade. Test on a tomato, not your thumb.

Don't run a good knife through the dishwasher. The heat and detergent wreck the edge you just built.

No stone yet?

A ceramic mug's unglazed bottom ring works as a stopgap. Pull the edge across it at the same angle, 15 passes a side.

  4. Repeat if needed. For stubborn clogs, do it twice. If it's still slow, use a plunger or a drain snake.

This works best on grease and soap scum. For hair clogs, a drain snake is more effective.

  • A soft cloth or paper towel
  1. Trace over the permanent marker. Use a dry erase marker to draw directly over the permanent lines. Let it sit for a few seconds.

The dry erase marker trick works on most non-porous surfaces, including glass and laminated schedules.

Crispy Roast Chickpeas

Prep 10 minOven 40 minMakes 2 cups
The whole trick is dry beans and a hot oven. Wet beans steam. Steamed beans are sad.
  • 2 cans chickpeas (15 oz each)
  • 2 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 tsp fine salt
  • 1/2 tsp smoked paprika
  • 1/4 tsp garlic powder
  1. Heat oven to 400°F / 205°C. Rack in the middle.
  2. Drain and rinse the chickpeas. Spread them on a clean towel and rub until they look matte. Loose skins can go in the bin.
  3. Let them air-dry 10 minutes while the oven heats. This matters more than any spice.
  4. Toss with oil and salt on a rimmed sheet pan. Spread into a single layer with space between them.
  5. Roast 35–40 min, shaking the pan at 20 min. Pull them when they rattle and one cracks open easily.
  6. Toss with paprika and garlic powder after roasting, while hot. Spices added early burn.
Keeping them crispy

Cool completely on the pan, then store in a jar with the lid loosely on. A sealed jar traps steam and they go chewy by tomorrow. If they soften anyway, 5 minutes back in a 400°F oven fixes them.

Reset a Tripped Breaker

2 minNo tools neededRead the safety note first
If you see scorch marks, smell burning, or the breaker is hot to the touch, stop and call an electrician. Do not reset it. Water plus electricity is also a call-someone situation.
  • A flashlight or your phone light
  • Dry hands and dry floor
  • One hand only, if you can manage it
  1. Find the panel. It is usually a grey metal box in a garage, hallway, or closet.
  2. Open the door. Look for a switch that sits between ON and OFF, or one that is clearly flipped the other way from its neighbours.
  3. Unplug whatever was running in the dead room. Space heaters and hair dryers are the usual suspects.
  4. Push the breaker firmly to OFF first, then all the way to ON. You should feel a solid click.
  5. If it holds, plug things back in one at a time. If it trips again on the same item, that item is the problem.
It tripped again immediately

That means the fault is still there. Leave the breaker OFF, unplug everything on that circuit, and try once more. Still tripping with nothing plugged in? The wiring itself needs a pro. Cheaper than a fire.

Passport Photo at Home

Setup 10 minFreeRules vary by country
Check your country's exact spec first. Sizes differ (US 2x2 in, UK 35x45 mm, and so on), and the photo is usually rejected for the little things, not the big ones.
  • Plain white or off-white wall
  • Bright, even light facing you
  • Phone on a steady surface
  • Plain dark shirt
  • A friend, or a timer
  1. Stand about 1 metre from the wall so you don't cast a shadow on it.
  2. Face a window or lamp. No light behind you, no flash glare on your glasses.
  3. Have the helper hold the phone at eye level, not chin level. Arm's length away.
  4. Look straight at the lens. Neutral face, mouth closed, both eyes open and visible.
  5. No glasses (many countries now ban them), no hats, no hair over your eyes or eyebrows.
  6. Shoot several. Pick the one where your head fills most of the frame with a little headroom.
  7. Crop to spec with a free passport-photo tool or your phone's editor, then print at a pharmacy or copy shop.
Common rejection reasons

Shadows on the wall, a tilted head, smiling with teeth, a patterned background, glare on glasses, or a photo that's slightly too zoomed in. Fix the shadow and the tilt first. That's most of them.

Stripped Screw, No Drill

5–15 minTry in order
Work through these gentlest-first. Stop as soon as one bites, so you don't make the head worse.
  • Wide rubber band
  • Flat-head screwdriver one size up
  • Hammer or the handle of a tool
  • Pliers or locking pliers
  • Optional: a little baking soda and superglue
  1. Lay the rubber band flat over the screw head. Press the screwdriver in hard and turn slowly. The rubber fills the gap and gives grip.
  2. If that fails, press the tip of a slightly larger flat-head driver into the slot and tap the handle once with a hammer to seat it. Then push down hard while turning. Pressure is what stops it slipping.
  3. If the head sticks up above the surface, grab it with locking pliers and turn the whole screw out. Slow, steady, no jerking.
  4. Last resort: clean the head, put a dab of baking soda in the slot, add a drop of superglue, press the screwdriver in, and hold 60 seconds. Let it cure fully before turning.
Why it stripped in the first place

Almost always the wrong bit size or not enough downward pressure. Next time, match the driver tip to the slot exactly and lean into it. A screwdriver that fits won't slip.

Ants in the Kitchen

15 min setupThen wait 3–5 days
Kill the trail and you kill the problem for a week. Kill the nest and you kill it for good. That's why bait beats spray.
  • Soapy water in a spray bottle
  • Ant bait gel or bait stations
  • Vinegar
  • Caulk or petroleum jelly
  • Sealed containers
  1. Follow the trail to find where they enter. It's usually a tiny gap at a window, baseboard, or pipe.
  2. Wipe the trail with soapy water or vinegar to erase the scent line. Do this after placing bait, or you'll clean up the bait smell too.
  3. Place bait stations right beside the trail, not in the middle of it. The ants need to find it and carry it home.
  4. Resist squashing the ones you see. They're the delivery service. Let them work for 3–5 days.
  5. Seal the entry gap with caulk. A smear of petroleum jelly works as a temporary barrier.
  6. Move sugar, cereal, and pet food into sealed containers. Crumbs under the toaster count.
It's been a week and they're back

You probably baited one trail and missed a second entrance. Follow the new line. If ants keep appearing with no visible trail, check behind the dishwasher and under the sink, then re-bait and give it another few days.
